extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners conducting 35 U.S.C. 101 subject matter eligibility (SME) analyses
extracted.subtask_description: A claim-by-claim USPTO examiner worksheet to determine subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 following the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (Steps 1, 2A, and 2B). It guides identification of the invention, statutory category, whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea), and whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what applicant invented and establish BRI
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention (MPEP 2103(I)). Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specification to determine what the applicant invented; every claim must be examined individually based on the particular elements recited therein, and a separate worksheet should be used to analyze each claim. The use of this worksheet is optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category check (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A or B: A) Yes — continue SME analysis. B) No — make a rejection of the claim as being drawn to non-statutory subject matter (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01). If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue SME analysis under that assumption and make the assumption clear in the record; consider suggesting a possible amendment to applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the claim directed to an abstract idea? (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the claim limitation(s) that correspond to an abstract idea and explain how such is similar to concepts previously held by the courts to be abstract. A claim is 'directed' to an abstract idea when the abstract idea is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found certain concepts to be 'abstract ideas', for example fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves (standing alone), or mathematical relationships/formulae. Identify limitations and explain similarity to judicial holdings (refer to the Quick Reference Sheet). Choose A, B, or C: A) No — conclude SME analysis. B) Yes, but streamlined analysis appropriate — eligibility self-evident; conclude SME analysis. C) Yes — identify limitations and continue to Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: When the eligibility determination is self-evident, a full eligibility analysis is not needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use streamlined analysis (Step 2A choice B) where applicant's claimed invention is not focused on the abstract idea and the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up an abstract idea such that others cannot practice it. Refer to the February 2015 Training Slides for examples of a streamlined analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify limitations that set forth the abstract idea and explain why
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly identify the steps/limitations in the claim that 'set forth or describe the abstract idea' and explain why those limitations are abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how the limitations correspond to abstract-idea concepts (e.g., 'the steps of receiving, filtering, and generating describe manipulating information by comparing and sorting the information based on a subscriber’s preferences' — 'These steps describe the abstract idea of comparing and organizing information for transmission'). Note that 'specifying the type of information being manipulated' does not render the idea less abstract. Cite analogous cases (e.g., Cyberfone, SmartGene) as guidance. Remember: 'Judicial exceptions need not be old or long-prevalent.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional elements beyond the abstract idea (Step 2B A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the abstract idea identified in Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose 1 or 2: 1) No — conclude SME analysis by making a § 101 rejection and continue with other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). Identify whether elements in the disclosure could be added to make the claim eligible and consider suggesting them to applicant. 2) Yes — list the additional claim elements (e.g., 'a transmission server with a memory that stores subscriber preferences and a microprocessor that performs the steps...'). Continue to evaluate significance under Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the additional elements, individually or in combination, provide an 'inventive concept' such that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reasons supporting the significance of additional elements, which can include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic computer functions); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending routine activities at a high level); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations that amount to more than generally linking the use of the abstract idea to a particular technological environment. Anti-patterns: merely adding 'apply it' language, generic computer functions, field-of-use limitations, or mere data gathering do not amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of elements individually and in combination; outcome determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the evaluation by deciding whether additional elements, taken individually or as a combination, result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Yes — conclude SME analysis and continue with other patentability requirements (explain reasoning in Office action if helpful). If No — conclude the SME analysis by making a § 101 rejection and continue with other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). Note: 'absence of complete preemption does not equate to eligibility.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggesting claim amendments and identifying candidate disclosure elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to the claim that may make it eligible, and consider suggesting such amendments to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include disclosed elements that transmit the alert over a wireless communication channel to activate an application, cause display of the alert, and enable connection to a data source over the Internet — elements that may, in combination, provide meaningful limitations and solve an Internet-centric problem (analogous to DDR Holdings). Provide specific suggested claim language where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action drafting and sample rejection language
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding the claim is ineligible, include a clearly articulated § 101 rejection in the Office action with supporting reasons and sample language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample rejection language is provided (e.g., 'Claim 1 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception...'). Use appropriate form paragraphs (7.05, 7.05.015, 7.05.01) for Office Action text. If concluding eligibility, an explanation is not necessary unless clarification would benefit the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's burden and evidentiary guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must 'clearly articulate the reasons why the claimed invention is not eligible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While factual evidence that an idea is abstract is not required for a prima facie rejection, examiners are encouraged to cite any additional resources that support their rejections. Provide clear reasoning in the record; include citations to precedent or training materials as appropriate.
